papers.title: BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
papers.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.

ai.reason: Compact self-supervised EEG model with arbitrary electrode support, transfer to sleep staging and low-resource wearables, directly matching interests in lightweight, generalizable, cross-recording EEG methods.
ai.summary: Introduces BrainCodes, a lightweight EEG foundation model pretrained via self-supervised learning on over 800 hours of recordings from more than 1,000 participants, combining a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder supporting arbitrary electrode configurations. It matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance on sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters, and transfers to low-resource wearable devices.

papers.title: NED-Net: an annotation-training loop for rodent EEG event detection
papers.abstract: Long-term EEG monitoring is central to rodent epilepsy research, and manual review is laborious because recordings span hundreds to tens of thousands of animal-hours. Published automated detectors perform well on their development datasets but are typically fixed models that may not adapt to another laboratory's electrodes, animals, or noise conditions. We introduce NED-Net, open-source software for training and maintaining seizure detectors. It uses reviewed candidate events as training labels, runs detection live during recording, and retrains as annotations accumulate. A detector trained on one mouse cohort (867 annotated seizures) achieved 93.6% precision in human review of 171 detections. Applied unchanged to a second cohort on the same acquisition system, its detections were mostly seizures (12 of 13 reviewed), but per-animal recall varied substantially (median 10%), with no convulsive reference seizure detected in four of 11 animals. Retraining with annotations from the second cohort raised convulsive recall from 15% to 64%, with at least one reference seizure detected in every animal. On recordings withheld from training, 75% of detections were seizures and 14 of 22 reference seizures were detected, whereas the source model and a model trained without these animals detected none. NED-Net supports evaluating and adapting detectors to local recordings.

papers.title: Subject-independent classification of ADHD from pediatric EEG: a leakage-aware deep learning framework with interpretable neurophysiological mapping.
papers.abstract: The use of electroencephalography (EEG) in automated screening of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) has created a large body of literature that suggests promising outcomes, with reported classification accuracies often above 90%. A major methodological issue suggests that a substantial part of these results are actually due to data leakage, whereby EEG epochs pertaining to the same subject end up in both training and testing sets, allowing classifiers to capitalize on features specific to the individual rather than on genuine disorder-related biomarkers. We assessed the performance of three classical machine learning algorithms, namely, Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), as well as three deep learning models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and CNN-BiLSTM, on a standard pediatric EEG dataset containing 121 children and 4,173 epochs. The performance of each model was compared in terms of both segment-wise cross-validation (Protocol A) and subject-wise cross-validation (without any data leakage, Protocol B).To evaluate neurotopographic plausibility without making unsupported causal assertions, we applied Deep SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to the best-generalizing architecture. The performance discrepancy was substantial. Under segment-wise evaluation, the SVM operating on power spectral density (PSD) features reached 90.0% accuracy (95% CI: [89.1%, 90.9%], AUC = 0.96). However, the same model dropped to 65.6% (95% CI: [62.1%, 69.1%], AUC = 0.72) under subject-wise evaluation-a statistically significant 24.4 percentage point collapse (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank). In contrast, deep architectures learning directly from raw EEG were resilient: the stand-alone CNN lost only 2.5 percentage points, achieving 72.7% accuracy (95% CI: [66.0%, 79.4%], AUC = 0.72, recall = 88.0%) on completely unseen participants. Post-hoc SHAP attribution identified the highest relative contributions in frontal (F3, Fz, F4) and central (Cz) electrodes, aligning with established ADHD neurophysiology. Hand-engineered spectral features are highly vulnerable to identity leakage, whereas end-to-end convolutional models generalize across subjects with realistic, uninflated performance. Strict subject-wise validation is strongly recommended as standard practice for translational EEG research.

ai.reason: Directly addresses subject-wise vs segment-wise validation leakage and interpretable neurophysiological mapping, highly transferable to EEG/animal state classification and reproducible ML practice.
ai.summary: Compared classical ML and deep learning models for pediatric ADHD EEG classification under segment-wise versus leakage-free subject-wise cross-validation; SVM on power spectral density features fell from 90.0% to 65.6% accuracy, while a raw-EEG CNN retained 72.7% on unseen participants, with SHAP attributions highlighting frontal (F3, Fz, F4) and central (Cz) electrodes.

papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

papers.title: Portable polysomnography-derived multi-domain EEG markers of anesthetic state transitions during propofol anesthesia for gastrointestinal endoscopy.
papers.abstract: Propofol anesthesia is widely used for gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, but electroencephalographic (EEG) features of anesthetic state transitions in this brief and stimulus-rich setting remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to describe clinically interpretable EEG markers across anesthetic stages using portable polysomnography (PSG)-derived six-channel EEG. In this prospective observational study, 31 adults undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol-based anesthesia underwent continuous portable PSG recording. EEG analyses focused on six scalp channels (F3, F4, C3, C4, O1, and O2) across four clinically defined stages: baseline, induction, maintenance, and recovery. Relative spectral power, spectral edge frequency at 95% cumulative power (SEF95), and spindle-like event metrics were quantified. Sensor-level functional connectivity was assessed using weighted phase-lag index, imaginary coherence, and amplitude envelope correlation (AEC). Spectral and spindle-like event measures were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, and connectivity differences were assessed using permutation-based paired tests with false discovery rate correction. Relative delta power decreased from baseline and induction to maintenance and recovery, whereas theta, alpha, sigma, and beta relative power and SEF95 generally increased. Spindle-like event density differed across stages and was highest during recovery, while mean duration and peak frequency remained relatively stable within the 11-16 Hz range. Functional connectivity showed metric-specific modulation: AEC demonstrated the most widespread stage-related differences, whereas phase-based connectivity measures showed only limited edge-specific changes after correction for multiple comparisons. Portable PSG-derived six-channel EEG captured stage-related spectral, spindle-like event, and sensor-level connectivity changes during propofol anesthesia for GI endoscopy. These findings identify candidate EEG features for future evaluation of emergence detection and atypical anesthetic-state identification during procedural anesthesia. Their utility for real-time propofol titration or excessive-sedation warning requires prospective validation.

Amplitude envelope correlation showed the most widespread stage-related connectivity differences, identifying candidate EEG markers for emergence detection and atypical anesthetic-state identification.

papers.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
papers.abstract: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

Synchronization reduced median timing error between EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms.

papers.title: Associations Between Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances have been implicated as a risk factor for developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), but evidence linking plasma AD biomarkers to sleep in cognitively unimpaired individuals remains limited. The present study examined associations between evening, morning, and overnight changes in plasma AD biomarkers and measures of sleep macro- and microstructure and subjective sleep quality in older adults. Forty cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 75 years (20 females) without sleep or mental disorders underwent overnight polysomnography. Plasma AD biomarkers p-tau181, p-tau217, t-tau, Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/40 were assessed in the evening and in the morning and related to sleep macro- and microstructure (sleep spindles, EEG spectral power), and subjective sleep measures by using correlational analyzes. Higher evening t-tau and p-tau181 were associated with reduced N3 sleep, whereas higher morning t-tau and greater overnight increases in t-tau were related to longer nocturnal wakefulness. Amyloid-β measures showed the most consistent associations with sleep microstructure. Higher Aβ42 and Aβ40 concentrations were associated with shorter duration and lower density of sleep spindles, particularly at frontal sites. Higher evening and morning amyloid-β concentrations were also associated with lower alpha, beta, and spindle-frequency EEG power, mainly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tau associations with EEG spectral power were less consistent. In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma AD biomarkers were associated with PSG sleep features, especially amyloid-β markers with sleep microstructure. These exploratory, correlational findings suggest that sleep spindles and spectral power may reflect early AD-related biological processes but require replication in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Multi-Metric EEG Connectivity and Graph Analysis Reveal Altered Resting-State Networks in Major Depressive Disorder.
papers.abstract: EEG functional-connectivity studies in major depressive disorder (MDD) have produced inconsistent findings, partly because different estimators capture distinct aspects of neural coupling. We implemented a multi-metric resting-state EEG approach combining linear, phase-based, nonlinear, and graph-theoretical measures to characterize frequency-dependent sensor-level connectivity alterations and identify sensor-level network patterns relevant to depression-related dysconnectivity. Resting-state EEG from 30 DSM-IV MDD participants and 28 healthy controls was analyzed using a 19-channel 10-20 montage. After MNE-Python preprocessing, including filtering, ICA-based artifact removal, current source density (CSD) transformation, and symmetric orthogonalization, coherence, PLV, PLI, and MI were computed across theta, alpha, and beta bands. Edge-wise differences were tested using Brunner-Munzel with Holm correction, confirmed with Westfall-Young maxT correction, and summarized using Hedges' g and graph measures. MDD showed frequency- and metric-dependent sensor-level connectivity alterations. Theta coherence, PLV, and PLI were dominated by lower connectivity across frontal-to-posterior, fronto-central, temporal/posterior-temporal, parieto-occipital, and central-to-occipital sensor pairs, whereas theta MI showed few increased frontal/fronto-temporal effects. Alpha findings were more selective, with mainly lower coherence and PLV across frontopolar/frontal-to-central, fronto-midline, and posterior links, while alpha MI showed a limited mixed pattern. In beta, coherence, PLV, and PLI showed sparse robust reductions, whereas beta MI showed widespread increased statistical dependence. Graph-theoretical summaries at 20% proportional density showed mainly lower mean weighted strength and global efficiency in theta- and alpha-band networks. These findings indicate frequency- and metric-dependent resting-state EEG sensor-level connectivity alterations in MDD. The dominant pattern was lower theta/alpha connectivity across distributed sensor pairs, alongside increased beta MI-based dependence. The results provide corrected, effect-size-informed evidence of altered inter-sensor coordination without establishing dysfunction of specific cortical regions or named networks. This framework may support future hypothesis-driven research in independent, clinically annotated, higher-density EEG or multimodal datasets.

papers.title: MULTIMODAL EEG WORLD MODEL: SELF-SUPERVISED LATENT TRANSITION LEARNING FOR WEARABLE EEG SEIZURE DETECTION
papers.abstract: Existing supervised and self-supervised EEG models mainly learn within-segment discriminative or reconstructive representations, leaving transitions between adjacent EEG segments underexplored. We propose a self-supervised Multimodal EEG World Model for EEG seizure detection that predicts the latent representation of the next EEG segment from the current EEG state, conditioned on synchronized ECG, EMG, and movement signals. A learnable query-based fusion module aggregates the multimodal synchronized signals into a compact physiological condition. Pretraining uses no seizure labels; downstream detection retains only the frozen EEG encoder and a linear probe. On the SeizeIT2 dataset with a strict patient-wise split, the model achieved an AUPRC of 0.3748, ROC-AUC of 0.8025, and balanced accuracy of 0.7308, outperforming official database baselines (SVM with hand-crafted features and ChronoNet), an external baseline (DSAINet), and a foundation model (NeuroLM). Ablations show a 14.4% relative AUPRC gain over a random-initialized encoder, supporting multimodal-conditioned latent transition learning for wearable EEG representation learning.

papers.title: MSANet: a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based driver fatigue recognition remains challenging because fatigue-related patterns are distributed across multiple temporal scales, inter-channel relationships vary across samples, and inter-individual differences complicate cross-subject transfer. To address these issues, a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network (MSANet) is proposed for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition. The framework introduces a multi-granularity patch temporal gate (MGPTG) to model locally continuous temporal contexts, stable graph node enhancement (SGNE) to enhance channel-node features before dynamic graph construction, and an adaptive classifier gate (ACG) to combine cosine-based and affine decision geometries. MSANet was evaluated on two public simulated-driving EEG datasets using a cross-subject transfer protocol, in which the target-subject samples were stratified with a partition ratio of 0.5 into a labeled adaptation subset and a held-out test subset. MSANet achieved an accuracy (ACC) of 83.64% and an F1-score (F1) of 83.74% on Dataset I, and 74.64% ACC and 72.92% F1 on Dataset II. The results indicate strong numerical performance on Dataset I and competitive performance on Dataset II. Subject-level statistical analysis was additionally conducted to distinguish mean performance differences from differences that are consistently supported across subjects. Ablation results showed lower mean performance after removing MGPTG, SGNE, or ACG under the evaluated settings. These findings support further evaluation of the proposed stage-specific temporal, graph-node, and classification mechanisms for cross-subject transfer in EEG-based driver fatigue recognition.

papers.title: Daytime Napping and Associative-Memory Retrieval Speed: An Exploratory Behavioral and EEG Study
papers.abstract: Purpose: To test whether a daytime nap was associated with improved associative-recognition performance relative to monitored wakefulness and to determine where any response-time (RT) difference occurred in the RT distribution. Methods: Fifteen healthy students completed nap and wake sessions in a within-participant design. Each session included word-pair learning, immediate recognition, a 60-min interval, and delayed recognition without additional study. Trial-level log RT was the focal outcome; accuracy and electroencephalography (EEG) were complementary outcomes. Results: The RT Condition-by-Time interaction was significant (b = -0.063, 95% CI [-0.117, -0.009], p = .027). Responses were 6.7% faster after the nap (p = .010) but did not change after wakefulness (p = .704), with the difference concentrated among slower responses. Accuracy showed no condition-specific change (p = .401). Nap EEG showed aperiodic spectral slowing and stronger periodic sigma activity, but no EEG measure explained the RT effect. Conclusions: Daytime napping was associated with faster delayed associative recognition, primarily through attenuation of the slowest responses. The exploratory findings warrant larger confirmatory studies.

Nap EEG showed aperiodic spectral slowing and stronger periodic sigma activity, but no EEG measure explained the response-time effect.

papers.title: A brain-behavior generative model links individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision speed varies across individuals and trials. Explaining this variability requires linking individual brain anatomy, neural dynamics, and behavior, yet whole-brain models typically reproduce brain signals without behavior, whereas behavioral models lack anatomical constraints. Here we introduce a brain-behavior generative model in which whole-brain dynamics on each participant's structural connectome generate both single-trial electroencephalography (EEG) and reaction times. Fitted to 17 participants performing motion discrimination, the models reproduced individual event-related potentials and reaction-time distributions. Joint fitting enabled the models to predict whether held-out trials were relatively fast or slow within each stimulus condition. In silico silencing further predicted where, how, and when each person's brain controls decision speed. Sensorimotor regions affected decision speed consistently across most participants, whereas the same parietal region had opposite effects in different participants. These opposite effects reflected whether the region acted mainly through network dynamics or the decision readout. Temporal analyses suggested that early activity largely set decision speed, whereas late EEG mainly tracked the unfolding decision. These results show that brain-behavior generative modeling can link individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions and yield testable predictions of why decision speed varies across individuals and trials.

papers.title: Auditory sustained potential as a biomarker of language functioning in children with autism and its implication in clinical trials.
papers.abstract: Most children with autism have language impairment, however, its neural mechanisms are not well understood. A potential biomarker associated with language in autism is a 40Hz Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR) triggered by periodic click-trains which in electroencephalogram (EEG) evokes two types of responses - 40Hz steady-state gamma response (ASSR) and sustained potential (SP). Although these responses represent low-level auditory processing, they correspond to different stages of sound perception/analysis and are essential in processing of spectrally/temporally complex sounds. However, until now there were no studies focusing on the potentials of these responses in clinical trials. The present open-label pilot study evaluated the effects of the probiotic beverage supplement Bio-K+ in children with autism (N = 19). Participants were assessed at three timepoints: T0 (baseline), T14 (14 weeks after intervention), and T22 (8 weeks after intervention, post-supplementation follow-up assessment), including EEG 40Hz ASSR and behavioral phenotyping. First, at T0 we showed a reduction of SP amplitude in children with autism compared to controls, and this reduction was associated with lower speech/language/communication scores. Second, the amplitude of SP became significantly more negative during the probiotic supplementation period and, by T14, was no longer significantly different from the observed in TD controls. Finally, these changes in the amplitude of SP were associated with improvement in speech/language/communication scores. This study showed that the SP as well as its change was related specifically to speech/language/communication but not to other behavioral measures and has a potential to be used in future clinical trials.

papers.title: An attention-enhanced hybrid CNN-BiLSTM framework for multiclass epileptic seizure recognition using EEG signals.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) signal classification plays a pivotal role in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and the diagnosis of neurological disorders. However, the non-stationary, non-linear, and low signal-to-noise ratio characteristics of EEG signals make accurate feature extraction challenging. Conventional deep learning approaches often struggle to simultaneously capture localized transient patterns, deep temporal dependencies, and long-range contextual relationships within EEG signals. To address these challenges, an optimized end-to-end hybrid deep learning framework, termed CNN-BiLSTM-MHSA, is proposed for multiclass epileptic seizure recognition. The architecture sequentially integrates a multilayer one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for localized feature extraction, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for capturing forward and backward temporal dependencies, and a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) mechanism for dynamically emphasizing discriminative neurological events. Robust preprocessing includes Butterworth bandpass filtering, Z-score normalization, and data augmentation using Gaussian noise injection and amplitude scaling. The framework was evaluated on the UCI/Kaggle Epileptic Seizure Recognition dataset comprising 11,500 EEG segments distributed across five classes. The proposed framework achieved an overall accuracy of 98.83%, precision of 98.95%, recall (sensitivity) of 98.84%, F1-score of 98.90%, specificity of 99.71%, balanced accuracy of 98.84%, ROC-AUC of 99.80%, and PR-AUC of 99.72%. Class-wise accuracies exceeded 99% for most categories, with one seizure class achieving perfect recognition. Comparative evaluation further demonstrated that the proposed framework outperformed several recent state-of-the-art EEG seizure classification methods. The superior performance can be attributed to the complementary representation capabilities of the hybrid architecture. CNN layers effectively learn localized signal patterns, BiLSTM captures bidirectional temporal dependencies, and MHSA enhances the representation of long-range contextual relationships by assigning greater importance to informative temporal regions. The combination of robust preprocessing and data augmentation further contributes to improved generalization and classification reliability.

papers.title: Inter-subject correlations and their behavioral associations vary across movies: Implications for generalizability.
papers.abstract: Movie-watching functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has become increasingly popular in neuroscience. Movie-fMRI data are commonly analyzed using inter-subject correlation (ISC), which quantifies the similarity of neural time series across individuals. Differences in ISC during movie viewing have been associated with psychological traits and clinical diagnoses. However, most studies investigating group differences in ISC or ISC-behavior associations have drawn conclusions from a single movie. Because ISC is inherently stimulus driven, effects observed for one movie may not generalize to another. Yet, the extent to which ISC patterns and ISC-behavior associations depend on the specific movie being viewed has received limited systematic attention. Here, we analyzed three independent datasets comprising 318 subjects and 36 movies in total to quantify between-movie variability in ISC and assess its consequences for ISC-behavior associations. Across datasets, ISC varied between movies throughout the cortex. This variability was spatially heterogeneous: regions with stronger ISC showed greater between-movie variability. Movie-specific inter-subject representational similarity analysis revealed distinct spatial distributions of ISC-behavior associations, with little overlap between movies. This pattern was observed for two distinct behavioral constructs. These findings suggest that ISC-behavior associations can be strongly movie specific.

ai.reason: Addresses cross-dataset generalizability of a neural time-series similarity metric, which is conceptually transferable, but it is fMRI-based and not directly EEG/sleep-methods relevant.
ai.summary: Analyzing three datasets (318 subjects, 36 movies), this study found that inter-subject correlation (ISC) and ISC-behavior associations vary substantially across movies, with little overlap in spatial patterns, indicating that ISC findings may be movie-specific and challenging to generalize.

papers.title: Diaphragm 'atonia' during ictal and post-ictal apnoea: A case report.
papers.abstract: Ictal and post ictal central apnoea (ICA and PCA) are driven by suppression of brainstem respiratory drive and represent an electroclinical biomarker of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). While animal models have demonstrated a true 'atonic diaphragm' underlying seizure-related apnoea, no human polygraphic study has yet confirmed respiratory muscle 'atonia' with direct EMG recording. In this case report, we present a 26-year-old female with meningoencephalocele-associated temporal lobe epilepsy who underwent a video-EEG polygraphy integrated with surface EMG from intercostals muscles and the diaphragm. We recorded a left frontotemporal seizure with ICA and four consecutives PCA events, all accompanied by surface electromyographic silence of the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles. This case provide a human polygraphic evidence of diaphragm and intercostal muscles silence during ICA and PCA, confirming the cascade of respiratory inhibition through brainstem respiratory centres down to respiratory muscles themselves. Notably, muscles relaxation occurred despite the patient was awake and able to follow commands. papers.title: EEG microstate alterations in psychotic depression: prolonged microstate C duration and associations with psychotic symptoms.
papers.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features (MDD-Psy) represents a severe clinical subtype with distinct psychopathology, yet its underlying large-scale brain network dynamics, as measured by resting-state EEG microstates, remain poorly characterized. We compared 68 patients with MDD-Psy and 63 patients with MDD without psychotic features (MDD-NonPsy). Clinical assessment included the Kangduo Antidepressant Scale (KDAS) and the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS). Resting-state EEG microstate parameters (duration, time coverage, occurrence, and transition probabilities) were analyzed. Group comparisons employed Mann-Whitney U/t-tests with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. Correlations between microstate alterations and psychotic symptom severity were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation with FDR correction. The groups were comparable in age and sex. The MDD-Psy group exhibited significantly greater severity in thought disturbance, activation, and hostility (all p < 0.001). EEG microstate analysis revealed a significantly prolonged median duration of microstate C, putatively associated with salience-network-related activity in MDD-Psy (91.99 ms) versus MDD-NonPsy (85.56 ms; p-corr = 0.004). Altered transition probabilities characterized MDD-Psy, including increased B→A but decreased B→C and C→A transitions (all p-corr < 0.05). Furthermore, in the combined sample, the duration of microstate C positively correlated with thought disturbance (ρ = 0.243, p-FDR = 0.030), while the reduced B→C transition probability was strongly negatively correlated with both thought disturbance (ρ=-0.393, p-FDR < 0.001) and hostility. Within patients with major depressive disorder, the psychotic subtype is associated with a distinct pattern of aberrant resting-state brain network dynamics relative to the non-psychotic subtype, characterized by prolonged microstate C duration, commonly linked to salience network dynamics and reconfigured temporal transitions between the salience, visual, and auditory networks. The altered visual-to-salience network transition (B → C) demonstrated the most robust association with core psychotic symptom dimensions, including thought disturbance and hostility. These findings suggest that dysregulated dynamic coupling between perceptual processing and salience evaluation may represent a candidate neurophysiological indicator of psychotic features in depression. However, these results should be considered hypothesis-generating preliminary: the high rate of antipsychotic medication use in the MDD-Psy group, the absence of a healthy control group, and the cross-sectional design preclude tentative causal or specificity claims. Future longitudinal studies incorporating medication-naïve patients, healthy controls, and complementary neurophysiological markers are required to validate the clinical utility of these microstate alterations. papers.title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
papers.abstract: Background: Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored. Objectives: We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8-13 Hz), and beta power (13-30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse. Results: Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions. Conclusions: These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

papers.title: A multiverse analysis of stomach-brain coupling in humans
papers.abstract: The gastric-brain axis is a burgeoning field of neuroscience; however, inferences from neuroimaging research are often constrained by the high dimensionality of methodological choices potentially leading to disparate outcomes. This study addresses such concerns by performing a multiverse analysis of gastric-brain coupling in humans. We systematically evaluated 5,184 unique analytic pipelines using electroencephalography (EEG) and electrogastrography (EGG) data to survey the methodological sensitivity of gastric-brain coupling. Our results reveal that whilst analytic decisions influence the magnitude of observed coupling, at the group level the phenomenon remains relatively consistent across the parameter space. High inter-individual variance can, however, be observed. Coupling was observed in the alpha, theta, and beta bands, with the latter two bands showing coupling at the largest number of electrodes. Coupling across frequency bands was primarily seen in medial electrodes, with some left lateral coupling also observed. Overall, these findings suggest that EEG-EGG based measurement of gastric-brain coupling is likely to be consistent across a significant range of plausible analytic pipelines at the group-level in healthy participants, providing useful context for future studies.

papers.title: Neural dynamics of emotionally expressive piano performance: a single-case study.
papers.abstract: Understanding how expert performers translate expressive intent into sound remains a central question in the neuroscience of music. We recorded continuous 128-channel EEG from a professional, internationally active concert pianist during a concert-like, uninterrupted performance (~27 min) of six works by Bach, Beethoven, and Chopin. From the continuous recording, 99 two-second clean EEG segments were extracted and assigned to one of six previously validated performance-emotion categories based on independent listener evaluations (Joy, Peacefulness, Melancholy, Argumentative, Tension, Power). Each 2-s fragment contained 1,024 time points per channel, yielding 131,072 EEG data points. Cortical and subcortical source generators were reconstructed with standardized weighted Low-Resolution Electromagnetic Tomography (swLORETA), and activation was quantified both as frequency of occurrence and as dipole magnitude across three macro-regions (anterior, posterior, subcortical). A chi-square test on activation frequencies showed a significant association between cortical/subcortical region and emotional category. Repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed significant region- and emotion-dependent differences in dipole magnitude. Across virtually every emotional category, the left basal ganglia, left thalamus, and left precentral gyrus (BA4) emerged as the most consistently recruited generators, indicating a stable left-lateralized fronto-striato-thalamic axis subserving fine motor control within this performance. Superimposed on this stable motor substrate, emotion-specific modulations emerged: Joy was associated with the highest subcortical activation magnitude, while Melancholy showed the lowest subcortical magnitude together with a selective recruitment of right-hemisphere generators (right BA10, right somatosensory cortex, right insula), consistent with valence-based hemispheric asymmetry accounts. Pearson correlations further linked activation of the left basal ganglia, left thalamus, and left premotor cortex (BA6) to objective performance parameters (gestures per second, notes per phrase, acoustic intensity), suggesting that neurofunctional engagement scales with the motor complexity of the material performed. These findings provide a performer-side perspective complementary to models of music-evoked emotion largely derived from listeners, and suggest that, in this elite performer, expressive intent was instantiated in a specialized, left-dominant sensorimotor-limbic network modulated by affective valence. The study is complemented by animated audiovisual materials that dynamically trace the moment-to-moment evolution of LORETA source activity in synchrony with the unfolding musical passage.

papers.title: Sensorimotor cortex activity during cued gait differs in Parkinson's freezers and non-freezers
papers.abstract: Gait impairments are a major contributor to disability in patients with Parkinson's disease despite dopaminergic and neuromodulation therapies. External cues (e.g., visual targets, rhythmic auditory sounds) are commonly used to improve gait quality and reduce freezing of gait (FOG), yet their effectiveness varies across patients and contexts. Improved understanding of the neural mechanisms of cueing benefits is essential to personalize rehabilitation strategies and improve outcomes. We use mobile electroencephalography (EEG) to test the hypothesis that cues improve gait through engagement of voluntary motor control mechanisms to compensate for impaired gait automaticity. In addition, we investigate whether this mechanism is related to cueing benefits or freezing status. Eighteen PD patients with a history of freezing (PD-F), 21 patients without freezing (PD-NF) and 19 age-matched healthy controls (HC) walked overground under three conditions: normal walking, synchronizing to auditory cues, and stepping over visual cues. Stride-locked beta band (13-30 Hz) power dynamics in sensorimotor cortex were used to measure cortical control of stepping. Spatiotemporal gait parameters improved with cues in all groups. However, PD-F had smaller cue-related gains in speed and stride length when compared with PD-NF for both cue types, and did not improve gait speed with visual cues. EEG revealed greater contralateral sensorimotor cortex swing-phase beta suppression in PD-F than PD-NF patients, with visual cues eliciting the most robust response. In contrast, beta suppression with cues was less pronounced in PD-NF and HC, despite greater behavioral gains. In addition, engagement of sensorimotor cortex during visual cueing was associated with divergent gait effects across PD subgroups: In PD-NF greater beta suppression was associated with less gait improvement, whereas in PD-F the opposite was observed. These findings suggest distinct sensorimotor control mechanisms for cue utilization in PD-F and PD-NF, and indicate that engagement of voluntary motor control circuits may underlie cueing benefits primarily in PD-F.

papers.title: Integrating task-state electroencephalography and motor function for intelligent assessment of recovery status from prolonged disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: Accurately assessing recovery in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (PDoC) is essential for evaluating the therapeutic efficacy and optimizing clinical care. However, substantial individual variability and poorly understood recovery mechanisms render this task exceptionally challenging. We collected task-state electroencephalography and clinical records from 78 PDoC patients to develop an intelligent assessment framework. Power spectral densities (PSDs) and coherence values (CVs) derived from event-related potentials (ERPs) were extracted and integrated with motor function scores to construct a multidimensional feature set. Linear support vector machine (SVM) and logistic regression (LR) models were built and rigorously evaluated via leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was utilized for visual explanation. The LOOCV indicated that both LR and SVM achieved optimal, similar performance in integrating alpha-band features with motor function (Macro-Average F1-score [Ma-F]: 76.79% versus 75.54%). The Receiver Operating Characteristic curves (with Area Under the Curve values of 77.57% for LR and 72.82% for SVM) and Precision-Recall curves (with Average Precision values of 68.87% for LR and 59.85% for SVM) suggested that the framework performs stably. The reliability curves indicated that both models demonstrate good calibration and are reliable for assessment. The study provides preliminary evidence that alpha-band PSDs and CVs derived from ERPs potentially enhance the motor function assessment performance. This integrated paradigm provides a valuable indicator. Overall, our findings suggest that combining neuroscience with intelligent technology holds promise for improving personalized diagnosis and optimizing the PDoC management.

papers.title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

papers.title: Temporoparietal alpha dynamics shape feedback-based updating during social bargaining
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires weighting incoming feedback against more stable action policies, but the neural dynamics controlling this balance during social interaction remain unclear. Across 296 experimental sessions in 219 participants, we combined computational modeling, EEG, fMRI, diffusion MRI, and fMRI-guided rhythmic TMS during repeated social bargaining. Behavior was captured by complementary feedback-based updating and reputation-based adjustment, with reproducible individual differences in how instructed social context reweighted feedback. Feedback-based updating showed the clearest convergent neural signature: trial-by-trial updating was associated with alpha-beta dynamics and multivoxel representational structure in right temporoparietal cortex. Critically, rhythmic alpha-TMS over individually localized TPJ sites selectively reduced feedback-based updating relative to active arrhythmic stimulation, while increasing baseline offers and modulating anticipatory alpha activity. Functional and structural connectivity analyses further implicated a distributed temporoparietal-frontal network. Together, these findings link a specific computational operation-feedback weighting-to temporoparietal alpha dynamics and show that rhythmic perturbation alters its behavioral expression.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in intracranial electroencephalography for epilepsy management: Insights from AI in Epilepsy 2025.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides direct recordings of cortical activity and remains central to the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the high dimensionality and complexity of iEEG data increasingly challenge conventional visual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have accelerated quantitative analyses in electrophysiology, supporting localization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic decision-making in epilepsy. This article reviews recent advances in the application of AI to iEEG in epilepsy and in particular stereo-EEG, although the concepts discussed are broadly relevant across iEEG modalities. Although many of these approaches have shown encouraging results, the current evidence remains largely preliminary, with most studies being retrospective, single-center investigations that lack independent external validation. AI-based integration of iEEG with multimodal magnetic resonance imaging shows promise for improving surgical planning in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Concurrently, early studies suggest that AI-driven iEEG analysis may enhance epileptogenic zone identification by detecting subtle electrophysiological signatures, network interactions, and temporal dynamics. These multimodal frameworks emphasize distributed epileptic networks rather than isolated focal abnormalities. AI is also reshaping how iEEG-guided stimulation is designed and interpreted. Data-driven approaches have the potential to optimize stimulation parameters, predict network responses, and clarify mechanisms underlying diagnostic and therapeutic stimulation, laying the groundwork for adaptive, patient-specific neuromodulation. Beyond short-term epilepsy monitoring, AI applications increasingly incorporate continuous sensing, longitudinal network modeling, and integration with implantable neurotechnology platforms. Although these developments require prospective multicenter studies with external validation before widespread clinical implementation, advances in multimodal data integration, interpretable modeling, and continuous sensing position AI-enhanced iEEG as an emerging platform for precision brain network medicine for epilepsy.

papers.title: [Neurophysiological differentiation of children with ADHD alone and ADHD comorbid with dyslexia: a P600-like component analysis].
papers.abstract: To investigate the clinical value of the latency of the P600-like event-related potential component during a spatial N-back task as a neurophysiological indicator for differentiating children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) alone from those with ADHD comorbid with developmental dyslexia (DD). In this prospective study, 66 ADHD children aged 6-10 years were enrolled from the Department of Child Health Care, Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University between June and September 2025, including 28 with ADHD alone and 38 with ADHD+DD. An additional 20 healthy children were included solely as a visual reference for electroencephalogram (EEG) topographic mapping. Behavioral symptoms were assessed using the SNAP-IV, the Childhood Executive Functioning Inventory, the Conners Child Behavior Scale, and the Dyslexia Checklist for Chinese Children. EEG was recorded during a spatial N-back task, and the P600-like component was extracted from Fz, Cz, and Pz electrodes. A linear mixed model was applied to analyze the interactions among group, electrode site, and task load. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to evaluate discriminative performance, and 5-fold cross-validation was conducted to reduce overfitting risk. Under the 1-back condition, the latency of the P600-like component at Pz was significantly longer in the ADHD+DD group than in the ADHD-alone group (P<0.001). The area under the curve (AUC) for the P600-like component latency at Pz in distinguishing ADHD alone from ADHD+DD was 0.804 (95%CI: 0.697-0.910). Using a cut-off value of 688 ms, sensitivity was 63.2% and specificity 96.4%. Hierarchical logistic regression analysis showed that model 4 (P600-like component latency + N1 reaction time + age) achieved an AUC of 0.804, comparable to that of model 2 (model 1 + P600-like component peak value + P600-like component average amplitude; AUC=0.805), with superior cross-validation stability. The latency of the P600-like component at the Pz electrode during an N-back task may serve as a neurophysiological indicator to assist in differentiating whether children with ADHD have comorbid DD. A parsimonious model incorporating this indicator has discriminative performance comparable to the full-indicator model, with superior cross-validation stability.

papers.title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction
papers.abstract: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.

papers.title: Validating electrical stimulation through the somatosensory system: a perspective on mismatch negativity and auditory prostheses.
papers.abstract: Natural touch engages specialized mechanoreceptors, while electrotactile stimulation bypasses them, directly depolarizing a mixed and non-uniform population of afferent axons. Whether this difference in peripheral encoding affects the brain predictive processing remains an open empirical question. The mismatch negativity (MMN), an established electroencephalography (EEG) marker of automatic change detection, provides a powerful tool to address this question without perceptual confounds. Somatosensory studies comparing MMN responses to natural versus electrical stimulation within the same healthy individuals can identify candidate mechanisms for testing in the auditory domain, where such designs are inherently not feasible. In particular, they can help disentangle device effects from deafness-related confounds in cochlear implant (CI) users. Existing somatosensory evidence in healthy subjects suggests that electrotactile stimulation elicits mismatch responses with less bilateral integration than natural touch, though this evidence remains limited to a single magnetoencephalography (MEG) study using an oddball paradigm. CI studies are more extensive and show feature-specific MMN deficits. However, they also rely on oddball or multi-feature paradigms that conflate prediction error with sensory adaptation. This Perspective therefore encourages the adoption of alternative MMN paradigms (roving, omission, or local-global) to determine whether electrical stimulation truly engages the brain's predictive machinery. With emerging multimodal stimulators, the somatosensory system offers a valuable platform to test whether electrical stimulation reproduces natural predictive processing-insights that can improve both tactile neuroprostheses and CI devices.

papers.title: N-back electroencephalography asymmetry and peripheral immune cell subpopulation composition.
papers.abstract: Cognitive deficits such as working memory impairment and peripheral inflammation frequently occur together in neuropsychiatric conditions, yet the relationship between them remains poorly understood. The aim of this study is to investigate whether the relative proportions of peripheral immune cell subpopulations are associated with EEG asymmetry during a working memory task and with task performance. EEG data were recorded from 24 healthy participants during a 2-back working memory task. Relative EEG asymmetry indices were computed for four frequency bands: alpha, beta, delta, and theta. 2-back task performance was also calculated. Peripheral blood was collected for DNA extraction and genome-wide DNA methylation analysis to estimate the relative proportions of immune cell subpopulations. Estimated proportions were Center Log-Ratio-transformed. Spearman's correlation and multiple linear regression were used to identify associations between EEG asymmetry, relative immune markers, and n-back task performance. Our analysis revealed that theta asymmetry was associated with CLR-transformed proportions of natural killer cells (p=0.035) and CD4+ T cells (p = 0.027). 2-back task target accuracy was nearly correlated with granulocytes (p = 0.082) and CD8+ T cell proportions (p=0.016); however, these associations did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction. Despite this, both immune markers significantly predicted 2-back target accuracy across three multiple linear regression models (model 1: p = 0.005, model 2: p = 0.002, model 3: p = 0.002).

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

We applied 20 Hz tACS (1 mA) for 30 min over the frontal cortex (F3 and F4, International 10-20 system) in 28 patients with DOC. Offline functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to quantify hemoglobin (HbO)-based functional connectivity (FC) and graph-theoretical network properties, including small-world properties (clustering coefficient, Cp; path length, Lp) and global efficiency (global efficiency, Eg; local efficiency, Eloc) at pre-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (pre-stim), the first post-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (post-stim1), and the second post-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (post-stim2). Subgroups were defined by baseline video-electroencephalography (vEEG) pathology as moderately abnormal (n = 11) and diffuse slowing (n = 14); 3 patients excluded (incomplete vEEG). Frontal 20 Hz tACS was associated with transient enhancement of FC across the measured cortical network at post-stim1 (pFDR < 0.05), selectively strengthening intra-and interhemispheric and intra-nodal connectivity before resolving by post-stim2. Frontal beta-tACS was associated with state-dependent changes in functional network organization in DOC, with dynamic fNIRS measures that may be useful for tracking these changes. papers.title: Automated Interpretation of EEG Reports Using a Large Language Model with Structured Confidence Outputs
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate a large language model (LLM) pipeline for extracting structured diagnostic labels and confidence levels from unstructured free-text EEG reports, addressing the barrier of narrative data analysis. Methods: We developed a hierarchical schema classifying reports for four abnormality types using a four-point confidence scale. Two certified EEG technologists annotated the reports independently; one was designated the Reference Annotator (RA) and the other the Second Annotator (SA). We implemented a grammar-constrained Mistral-7B pipeline and evaluated its agreement with the RA alongside the SA and classical NLP baselines using Core Agreement and Certainty-Adjusted Agreement. A portability analysis held the task, labels, output grammar, report identifiers, reference annotations, and endpoints fixed while a MedGemma configuration used its model-declared instruction-turn format. Results: For overall abnormality, Mistral-7B achieved 96% Core Agreement with the RA and the SA achieved 98%. Mistral-7B exceeded the tested low-resource baselines in most categories and identified rare epileptiform abnormalities for which the baselines produced no or few true positives. Among reports with matching overall-abnormality decisions, Conditional Certainty Agreement was about 80% for Mistral--RA on each evaluated report set and 90% and 94% for SA--RA. The MedGemma configuration showed higher agreement than Mistral-7B in several non-epileptiform categories, but focal epileptiform performance involved a trade-off between missed and additional positive calls. Conclusions: Under the studied report-level conditions, the grammar-constrained pipeline produced structured annotations with high binary agreement to the RA. After adapting the prompt presentation to its model-declared instruction-turn format, the same structured task and evaluation framework transferred to a newer local model. The results support its use as a research annotation method; they do not establish diagnostic ground truth, external validation, or readiness for clinical deployment. Significance: This study demonstrates a locally executable method for converting de-identified EEG narratives into structured research annotations while retaining an ordinal representation of annotator certainty.

papers.title: Behavioural expression of ictal embarrassment: a stereo-EEG case report.
papers.abstract: Embarrassment is a rare ictal manifestation whose neurophysiological basis remains poorly understood. We describe the case of a 40-year-old woman with drug-resistant focal epilepsy characterized by an unusual ictal semiology combining an intense positive emotional experience with behavioral manifestations of embarrassment. Stereo-EEG demonstrated seizure onset within the middle frontal gyrus bank of the superior frontal sulcus (F2sb), with rapid propagation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and superior anterior insula (sAI). Electrical stimulation of the F2sb reliably reproduced the habitual electroclinical seizure. While identical stimulation parameters elicited the subjective and autonomic manifestations in both supine and upright postures, the complete behavioral repertoire of embarrassment emerged only when stimulation was delivered in the standing position. Exploratory functional connectivity analyses revealed that overt embarrassment was associated with reduced node strength within a network encompassing the dACC, sAI, mesial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). More restricted network changes were associated with only mild sensations, whereas asymptomatic stimulation produced a distinct and partly reversed connectivity pattern. This case suggests that the behavioral expression of ictal embarrassment arises from the transient reconfiguration of a frontal-cingulo-insular network and is critically shaped by bodily context.

papers.title: Motor network neurophysiological (TMS-EEG) markers as predictors of outcomes of ventriculoperitoneal shunt sustained for over a year in normal pressure hydrocephalus.
papers.abstract: Current practice for normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) relies on clinical presentation, imaging, and various clinical procedures to determine the need for neurosurgical intervention, specifically the installation of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS). This study aimed to evaluate the utility of a TMS-evoked potential (TEP)-based assessment (Delphi-MD) for predicting sustained response (over one year) to VPS, serving as an ancillary test to the cerebrospinal fluid tap test (CTT). Forty-one patients with possible iNPH underwent Delphi-MD evaluation of wave form adherence (WFA), a composite measure assessing how closely their TEPs resembled an ideal benchmark TEP. Of these, 18 patients received VPS treatment following a multidisciplinary team decision based on standard practice, blinded to the TEP results. Response to the intervention was evaluated over a period of more than one year using the clinical global impression of change (CGIC) scale, in addition to assessments with a 10-meter timed up and go test and the modified Rankin scale. Responders had higher M1L WFA values at baseline (prior to VPS) than non-responders (median 0.51 [95% CI 0.36-0.76], median 0.14 [95% CI -0.02-0.38], respectively p = 0.012). M1L WFA was successful in distinguishing responders (11/18) from non-responders (7/18) with an ROC-AUC of 0.935 [bootstrap 95% CI 0.792-1.00], p < 0.0001. M1L WFA cutoff was established with LOOCV and produced 90.9% sensitivity, 85.7% specificity and 88.9% accuracy. In contrast the CTT result was unsuccessful in predicting shunt responsiveness. This study indicates that higher M1L WFA obtained through Delphi-MD (TMS-EEG), signifies better preservation and functional integrity of the motor network in patients with probable iNPH that had a sustained response to VPS than those that did not. Given replication of results in future independent cohorts, Delphi-MD shows promise as an objective, accurate, and accessible ancillary screening tool for iNPH candidates, prior to referral for VPS treatment. papers.title: Frontal Asymmetry in Infancy: Predictive Utility for Distinct Patterns of Temperament.
papers.abstract: Recent theorizing has emphasized motivational systems, rather than specific emotional reactions, when interpreting frontal asymmetry. We examined the predictive utility of infant electroencephalogram (EEG) frontal asymmetry during two approach-oriented tasks within 82 mother-infant dyads (infant age: M = 38.88 weeks, SD = 8.13 weeks; infant ethnicity: 86.7% Caucasian; infant sex: 51.2% female). Peek-a-Boo (PAB) and Toy Removal (TR) were chosen as predictors of mother-reported temperament, as both elicit approach motivation via a blocked goal in a joyful and frustrating context, respectively. TR asymmetry effect on Surgency/Positive Affectivity (SPA) was observed and driven primarily by a significant predictive relationship between TR asymmetry and Smiling and Laughter, f2 = 0.31. Negative Emotionality (NE) related outcomes were predicted by TR asymmetry, driven by Sadness, f2 = 0.20. Other than occasional contributions of covariates, no additional statistically significant results were noted. These findings are discussed as most consistent with the capability model of lateralization.

papers.title: Serotonin Neurobiology and Artificial Intelligence-Driven Biomarker Detection in Affective Disorders: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.abstract: Affective disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), impose a major global health burden because of their high prevalence, early onset, disability, and substantial social and economic impacts. Diagnosis remains challenging because it relies largely on subjective clinical assessment and symptom-based criteria, which often delay recognition and contribute to heterogeneous treatment response. Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) has long been central to the understanding of these disorders, but the classical serotonin hypothesis has evolved into a broader systems-level framework in which serotonergic dysfunction is linked with neurotransmission, receptor signaling, transporter regulation, neuroplasticity, endocrine balance, immune modulation, circadian rhythm control, and gut-brain communication. Serotonin biosynthesis, metabolism, and compartmentalization are tightly regulated, and variation in the serotonin transporter and related pathways influences vulnerability to disease, symptom expression, and response to therapy. Although serotonin-targeted pharmacotherapy remains foundational, its delayed and variable clinical effects highlight the need for objective biomarkers and more-precise monitoring strategies. This Review gives a comprehensive overview of serotonin neurobiology in affective disorders and the therapeutic implications of serotonergic dysregulation. It discusses the current understanding of serotonin synthesis, receptor heterogeneity, transporter function, and broader system interactions that shape mood, stress responsivity, and treatment outcomes. The Review also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in psychiatric biomarker discovery, including machine learning and deep learning approaches applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, physiological signals, and language-based data for improved diagnosis and prediction of antidepressant responses. In addition, emerging serotonin-specific biosensors are discussed as promising tools for real-time, noninvasive neurochemical monitoring. By integrating mechanistic insights into serotonin biology with AI-based analytics and biosensing technologies, this Review highlights a pathway toward more objective, personalized, and effective management of affective disorders.

papers.title: Psychedelics and Reward Processing: Before and After the 1970 Controlled Substances Act.
papers.abstract: This narrative review traces how the scientific understanding of psychedelics has intersected with "reward processing" from before the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) era to the present, emphasizing how cultural and regulatory climates shaped what was viewed as an acceptable research question. Reward processing is treated as a family of partially overlapping phenomena: (1) reward-linked behavior (e.g., self-administration, conditioned place preference, reinstatement), (2) reward-circuit signals (e.g., mesolimbic dopamine dynamics, electrophysiology, human electroencephalography potentials), and (3) clinically relevant outcomes in substance use disorder (SUD) (e.g., withdrawal severity, consumption, relapse). Across these measures, the literature repeatedly adopts two framing logics: "liability framing," which prioritizes misuse potential and dependence risk, and "therapeutic framing," which treats psychedelics as tools for probing and potentially reconfiguring reward circuitry and learning. Organized by decade, the review shows that the 1960s already contained both motifs, with adjunctive therapeutic hopes alongside early reinforcement assays, while the CSA era increasingly systematized a hazard-first posture that defined the late 1970s through the 2000s, referred to as the "psychedelic dark age." Within those constraints, monoamine and receptor pharmacology (including serotonin-dopamine interactions) became a dominant tool for investigating reward, and ibogaine programs loudly reintroduced a therapeutically oriented anti-addiction narrative. In the 2000s, serotonergic control of dopaminergic reward systems and entactogen models, including social reward, broadened the mechanistic frame. In the 2010s and 2020s, the field's momentum shifted toward therapeutic models, circuit plasticity, computationally interpretable reward signals, and renewed clinical work in SUD. The review argues that a central bottleneck is not a lack of provocative acute findings but rather a lack of experimental programs that bridge behavior, circuit signals, and longitudinal clinical endpoints. We therefore propose that revisiting important concepts and findings discussed herein with recently developed technology and approaches (e.g., cue-evoked signals, learning parameters, photometry) across dose, time, and sex would advance the field. We highlight practical study shifts to move toward an integrated account of how psychedelics modulate reward-relevant brain activity and behavior.

papers.title: Piezoelectric actuator-evoked mechano-gated currents in trigeminal neurons innervating the mouse temporomandibular joint.
papers.abstract: The most burdensome symptom of temporomandibular joint disorders (TMJDs) is mechanically evoked pain. To identify the trigeminal ganglion (TG) neuronal subtypes mediating mechanical sensitivity, we combined whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology with immunohistochemistry (IHC) to characterize mouse TMJ-innervating TG neurons retrogradely labeled from the TMJ. Electrophysiological analysis identified five distinct neuronal groups, only one of which responded to piezo actuator-induced mechanical stimulation. TMJ innervation was dominated by C- and A-nociceptors, comprising four of the five identified groups. The fifth, a minor population of small-diameter neurons (S1), displayed properties consistent with either vGlut3-positive, C-low-threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs) or Sst-positive neurons. Two mechanically insensitive C-nociceptor groups, distinguished by their action potential firing patterns, likely corresponded to CGRP-positive and non-Mrgpr neuronal populations. One mechanically insensitive A-nociceptor group likely represented Smr2-positive Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (Aδ-HTMRs). The only mechanically responsive neurons were large-diameter A-nociceptors, which likely correspond to the weakly TrkC- expressing neuronal population. No recorded neurons displayed electrophysiological characteristics of classical A-LTMRs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the TMJ is innervated by a distinct repertoire of TG sensory neurons compared with the skin and masseter muscle, with mechanically responsive afferents restricted to a single A-nociceptor subtype rather than classical low-threshold mechanoreceptors.

papers.title: Indolizine-Based Small-Molecule Fluorescent Probes for Ex Vivo Imaging of Amyloid-β Plaques.
papers.abstract: Fluorescence probes for visualizing amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques are important tools in Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. We synthesized a library of 49 indolizine derivatives using a modular synthetic approach and evaluated their fluorescence labeling behavior directly in ex vivo brain tissue sections from 5XFAD transgenic mice. Through an ex vivo tissue-based screening workflow using anti-Aβ antibody 6E10 as a reference standard for plaque-containing regions, five hit compounds (YIZ-20, YIZ-32, YIZ-36, YIZ-45, and YIZ-47) displaying plaque-associated fluorescence patterns were identified. Costaining experiments demonstrated spatial correspondence between probe fluorescence and antibody-defined plaque regions. Spectral analysis showed that the selected YIZ probes exhibited emission profiles with somewhat reduced overlap with the Hoechst 33342 channel compared with thioflavin S (ThS), providing a modest but practical advantage for multichannel imaging applications. These findings highlight the utility of ex vivo tissue-based screening for fluorescent-probe discovery and establish indolizine as a promising scaffold for the development of complementary fluorescence imaging tools for AD-related ex vivo tissue studies.
